endorsements.quote: If AI systems influence clinical outcomes, then responsibility must be distributed across the full chain of actors involved in their development and deployment, including developers, vendors, and institutions (Jobin et al., 2019 ).

Thus, human authority must be accompanied by continuous investment in clinically and culturally relevant training, reflexive practice, and institutional support structures that enable practitioners to navigate the complexities of AI-mediated clinical decisions with confidence and responsibility.
Thus, efforts to ethically govern AI in Africa should deliberately include ways to preserve the practitioner’s capacity to interpret, question, and challenge algorithmic outputs.
Moreover, and importantly, such an approach would also resist the tendency to treat ethical evaluation as a one-time pre-deployment exercise.

unlisted_practices: Conduct relational impact assessments of AI clinical decision support systems, evaluating effects on trust, epistemic agency, relational autonomy, local knowledge, responsibility, equity, and moral residue, iteratively across the AI lifecycle.

Co-produce AI knowledge with local practitioners, patients, caregivers, community representatives, and other relevant stakeholders in the design, validation, and governance of AI systems rather than merely locally adapting externally developed systems.
Align authority and accountability so that practitioners are not held responsible for AI decisions they cannot design, audit, or challenge.

screen.reason: This is a conceptual and ethical commentary paper proposing relational and context-sensitive AI governance frameworks and impact assessments for AI clinical decision support systems in Africa.
